Description:
A construct that derives an IDENTITY from a filesystem path without canonicalizing it first. Fires when the construct that MINTS a token (references projectToken) does not also reference a canonicalizer (CanonicalSourceRoot, EvalSymlinks).

The join is on node_refs.container_node_id — the ENCLOSING definition — not node_id. node_id is the call-site node (a deep .../call_expression/argument_list path), so joining on it asks 'does this one call expression contain another call', which is never true and made the first version of this rule fire on correctly-canonicalized code, including the very function that fixed mache-0e4773. Same column confusion that made find_callees empty on leyline projections (mache-cb8fb9).

Scoped to projectToken alone, not registerProject: canonicalization happens INSIDE registerProject, so flagging its callers would report the fix as the defect.

Why this is a rule and not a review habit: the same tree is reachable through more than one path — a symlink, a bind mount, a case-insensitive filesystem — and every layer that compares paths must agree on which of those spellings is canonical. mache already learned this three times independently (internal/leyline/arena_config.go canonicalizes and says why; internal/ingest/engine.go canonicalizes; leyline's own verify_source_root_matches compares Rust-canonicalized paths). The project registry was the one layer that did not, so `mache init` from ~/github/art/mache and from ~/remotes/art/mache minted two different tokens for one project (mache-0e4773).

The failure is one-directional, which is why it is worth a gate rather than vigilance. A too-COARSE identity — two projects colliding on one token — is caught loudly by leyline's cross-source warm-start refusal. A too-FINE identity — one project splitting across two tokens — is caught by NOTHING: each side stays internally consistent and they simply disagree. Reviewers reliably catch the loud one.

SCOPE, deliberately narrow. This does not flag every path use, which would be a brittle heuristic: most os.Getwd/filepath.Abs calls have nothing to do with identity and canonicalizing them would be noise. It flags only constructs that reach for a KNOWN identity-deriving function, so precision is high and the false-positive story is a short list rather than a judgement call. Extending it means adding a token to the IN clause when a new identity function appears — which is the point: the rule is a ledger of 'these functions mint identities', and forgetting to add one is a visible omission rather than a silent gap.

BINARY rule: no meaningful magnitude, so it emits 0 AS metric (the query contract still requires the column).

Known divergence: node_refs stores the bare call token, so a same-named method on an unrelated type would be a false positive — the same documented caveat the built-in sleep_in_test and fatal_call_in_library rules carry. Works on every backend (node_refs + nodes only, no _ast needed).

LOCATION: the finding points at the ENCLOSING construct's span, joined from _ast on container_node_id, emitting tree-sitter's RAW 0-based row/col: the engine converts to 1-based itself (cmd/smell_findings.go:107, `Line: startRow + 1`), so a rule that pre-converts double-counts. Verified empirically against ground truth rather than reasoned about — the first version reported the line above each declaration. Emitting 0 (as the binary-rule examples do) costs the reader the jump — a finding you cannot open is half a finding. This is why Requires lists _ast: the rule degrades to unavailable on a standalone projection rather than reporting a location it does not have.

GROUP BY/ORDER BY are POSITIONAL (1, 2), not by alias: node_refs and _ast both carry a source_id column, so the unqualified alias is ambiguous to SQLite and the rule fails to run at all with 'ambiguous column name'. A rule that errors is worse than one that is silent — the gate reports it as a rule failure, not as zero findings.

PRECISION: the ref site must have _ast node_kind = 'call_expression'. Without it the rule matched `httpServerEntry(projectToken)` — the token being PASSED as an argument (node_kind 'argument_list'), and a parameter named projectToken at that — rather than a call minting one. That is the structural discriminator the bare-token caveat above otherwise leaves open: node_refs records the name, _ast records what syntactic position it occupied. Name-matching alone cannot tell a call from an identifier; the parse tree can.
Query: SELECT COALESCE(n.source_file, a.source_id) AS source_id, r.container_node_id AS node_id, a.start_byte AS start_byte, a.end_byte AS end_byte, a.start_row AS start_row, a.start_col AS start_col, 0 AS metric FROM node_refs r JOIN nodes n ON n.id = r.node_id JOIN _ast a ON a.node_id = r.container_node_id JOIN _ast ref ON ref.node_id = r.node_id WHERE r.token IN ('projectToken') AND ref.node_kind = 'call_expression' AND COALESCE(r.container_node_id, '') != '' AND COALESCE(a.source_id, '') != '' AND a.source_id NOT LIKE '%%_test.go' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM node_refs c WHERE c.container_node_id = r.container_node_id AND c.token IN ('CanonicalSourceRoot', 'EvalSymlinks')) %s GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2
